title: Research in Complex Operational Contexts
summary: Research in complex operational contexts covers research programmes conducted in real or ecologically realistic operational settings, including sea trials, clinical testing, control rooms, clinics, machining cells, canteens, forecourts, and expert workplaces. It focuses on evidence that interviews or laboratory sessions alone cannot produce: workarounds, environmental constraints, role conflicts, tacit knowledge, and task structures under pressure.
keyFacts: Torqeedo maritime HMI research included 12 sea trials over 6 months with 15 professional captains in temperatures from −5°C to +35°C.
IDEXX Animana research covered 35 clinics, 150+ participants, 2 weeks, and 3 countries: the Netherlands, the UK, and Germany.
Triopsis research combined 43 user interviews, 21 participants, 3 in-situ observation sessions, 5 stakeholder interviews, and competitive benchmarking; 47 microtasks were mapped.

Gexcon CFD simulation research was preceded by domain learning and documented 102 individual tasks after 24 user interviews, 23 workplace observations, 9 stakeholder interviews, and benchmarking of 12 competitor products.
Swiss petrol forecourt research documented and coded 532 transactions from 40 hours of structured observation, with 36 cashiers observed and 24 interviews.
Squaremind research used deliberate unstructured observation before redesign and post-redesign ecological testing with an independent dermatologist, 29 users, and age-stratified cohorts.

Maritime VTS access to representative end-customer operators was negotiated as a release condition, and research used sanitised scenarios in operational VTS control rooms at a customer site rather than live traffic.
visioncheckout field research covered six locations across three organisations over five days, observing 563 interactions and measuring transaction durations with a clock.

bodySections.heading: What Research in Complex Operational Contexts Means
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Research in complex operational contexts is the study of expert or high-consequence work in the conditions where it is actually performed. Creative Navy uses field observation, domain learning, representative participant access, adaptive protocols, and multiple evidence sources to make operational reality available for design.

This capability is used when the operating environment is part of the system. The relevant evidence is not only what participants say in interviews. It includes what participants do under pressure, what they cannot articulate, what the environment prevents, and what workarounds have accumulated around interface failure.

bodySections.heading: When Operational-Context Research Is Needed
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Operational-context research is needed when design validity depends on real environments, representative participants, or live task conditions. In expert tools and high-consequence systems, non-expert participants can produce invalid findings because they do not encounter the actual cognitive, procedural, and environmental constraints of the work.

Participant access is therefore a research problem in its own right. Documented programmes include professional captains, surgeons, CFD engineers, schedulers, cashiers, NHS analysts, academic researchers, pharmaceutical research staff, VTS operators, clinical patients, catering staff, and machining-cell operators. The value of the research depends on reaching participants who actually perform the work, not substitutes who can only comment on it.

Operational-context research is also needed when participants cannot explain their own practice. The blanks phenomenon appears when participants cannot articulate the rationale for what they do. In those situations, direct questioning is not sufficient. Tacit knowledge has to be surfaced through observation, structured teaching methods, and comparison between what people say and what they do.

bodySections.heading: How Creative Navy Runs Operational-Context Research
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy uses domain learning before or alongside formal research when the domain is too specialised for generic research instruments to produce valid findings. Domain learning can include studying manuals, reviewing training material, testing the product directly, and using stakeholder sessions to establish workflow logic before user sessions begin.

Creative Navy uses in-situ observation when interviews are insufficient to expose work as performed. Observation can show how people handle incident conditions, conflicting priorities, overlapping jobs, environmental interference, and sudden changes that are difficult to reconstruct accurately through interview recall.

Creative Navy uses real-time protocol adaptation when early fieldwork reveals patterns that the original protocol did not anticipate. When workarounds or unplanned behaviours appear across sites, later visits can probe those patterns more directly rather than treating the protocol as fixed.

Creative Navy uses triangulation-not-confirmation when multiple evidence sources disagree. The purpose is not to collect parallel confirmations. The purpose is to set evidence sources against each other and treat discrepancies as findings.

bodySections.heading: What Operational-Context Research Produces
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Operational-context research produces research corpora that make complex design work tractable. These corpora may include documented tasks, microtasks, role differences, environmental constraints, workflow sequences, failure points, recovery behaviours, and baseline measurements.

Operational-context research can produce structural design requirements that would not appear in interviews. Examples include information stability under unpredictable vessel behaviour, role separation where a single persona would hide the central finding, and interface requirements shaped by physical placement, lighting, noise, posture, and machine state.

Operational-context research can also produce baseline documentation for later design evaluation. Transaction counts, timing measurements, error-resolution observations, completion data, and recovery behaviour can give later design work a reference point. Where figures describe the system being replaced, they should not be read as measured results of a redesign.

bodySections.heading: Evidence Base Across Domains
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The documented evidence base for this capability spans maritime systems, clinical devices, veterinary clinic software, workforce management, CFD simulation, petrol forecourt operations, maritime VTS control rooms, industrial automation, and self-checkout systems.

The evidence includes immersive field research, ecologically realistic testing, structured observation, unstructured observation where measurement would have produced noise, workplace observation, moderated requirements sessions, stakeholder interviews, competitive benchmarking, and timed observations.

The evidence is case-based. It supports the claim that operational-context research can reveal workarounds, tacit knowledge, role conflicts, environmental constraints, and task structures that interview-only or laboratory-only research may miss. It does not imply that every engagement requires the same research depth, participant count, or operational access.

bodySections.heading: Boundaries and Limits of the Capability
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Research in complex operational contexts does not include every interview, walkthrough, bench session, or late-stage review. The capability is specifically about research where operational setting, representative participant selection, environmental conditions, live task structure, or ecologically realistic scenarios are necessary for valid findings.

Some engagements use constrained operational substitutes rather than live operation. In maritime VTS research, Creative Navy observed operators in working control rooms using sanitised scenarios rather than live traffic. Both conditions matter: the control-room setting was operational, and the scenario data was not live traffic.

Some engagements deliberately avoid measurement at an early stage. In Squaremind pre-redesign research, unstructured observation was chosen because the existing patient interface was performing so poorly that systematic measurement would have produced noise rather than insight. Structured measurement was appropriate later, after the terrain was understood.

Some measured figures describe the system being replaced, not the redesign. In visioncheckout research, the observed timings describe the live system under replacement. They should not be read as measurements of new designs.

Field observations remain engagement-specific. The machining-cell findings from the industrial automation engagement describe that observed facility and should not be generalised to all industrial automation environments.

bodySections.heading: What this produces
bodySections.bodyMarkdown: Within Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method, this capability produces concrete interface design deliverables — interaction design, information architecture, wireframes, screen designs, interactive prototypes, and design-system components — and not advisory documents alone. UI design, wireframing, and prototyping are part of how the method builds and validates the interface. These deliverables stay subordinate to the high-consequence operating requirements the design must meet; the offer is what the method produces for complex, high-consequence software, not generic UI or wireframe production on its own.

strongClaims: Research in complex operational contexts studies expert or high-consequence work in the real or ecologically realistic conditions where design validity depends on operational reality.
Torqeedo maritime HMI research included 12 sea trials over 6 months with 15 professional captains in environmental conditions that could not be replicated elsewhere.
IDEXX Animana used real-time protocol adaptation when handwritten workarounds appeared across clinics.
Gexcon research required domain learning before formal research and produced a corpus of 102 documented individual tasks.
Swiss petrol forecourt research documented 532 transactions and recorded a peak transaction rate of 84 transactions per hour during field observation.
Squaremind research used deliberate unstructured observation before redesign and independent clinical co-validation during post-redesign ecological testing.
Maritime VTS research access to end-customer operators was negotiated as a release condition, and research used sanitised scenarios rather than live traffic.
visioncheckout field research observed 563 live interactions over five days and measured transaction durations with a clock rather than by estimate or self-report.
weakerClaims: Triopsis research showed that in-situ observation produced a more accurate picture of scheduling work under operational pressure than interviews alone.
limitations: The capability excludes engagements that did not conduct research in an operational context; interview-only, bench-session, no-observation, or late walkthrough evidence is not treated as contextual inquiry here.

Maritime VTS research used sanitised scenarios in operational VTS control rooms at a customer site; it did not use live traffic and participants did not issue navigation instructions or control radio equipment during sessions.
visioncheckout timing data describes the system being replaced and must not be read as a measured result of the redesign.
Squaremind pre-redesign observation was deliberately unstructured and did not produce measurement data; structured measurement appeared in the post-redesign ecological testing phase.
The industrial automation observations describe one observed machining-cell environment and should not be generalised to the whole industry.
